newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee at 20-year high in active commodities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee at 20-year high in active commodities.

text.p: Coffee futures prices hit a new 20-year record in New York on Wednesday on jitters about cold weather in Brazil at a time when stocks are already low and supply is tight from Latin America.
Elsewhere in active world commodity markets, the rare white metals, platinum and palladium, were sharply up on news of a strike at the big Rustenburg mine in South Africa.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, futures for arabica coffee beans for July delivery rose almost seven cents to $2.81 per pound, the highest for two decades.

Forecasts for cool winter weather in Brazil, the biggest exporter, did not point to a damaging frost. But they were enough to trigger new speculative buying in a rally that has lifted prices for American arabica coffees by 150 percent this year.

Less-prized robustas, from Africa and Asia, are in better supply. But the benchmark London July robusta contract was also higher on Wednesday and, at just below $2,200, was firmer by about 80 percent since January 1.
"Coffee is physically tight with stockpiles in both consumer and producer countries at 20 year lows, and this makes the market extremely prone to weather scares in Brazil...'said brokerage GNI Ltd.
Palladium which hit a record high official price on Wednesday, is the humblest of the precious metals. Most of it is hidden away in dental work or car exhaust sytems.

But prices for both palladium and its sister rare white metal, platinum, soared on Wednesday on news of a strike at South Africa's Rustenburg, the world's largest platinum mine, that followed five months of delay in exports by Russia, the biggest exporting nation.
Palladium was fixed in London at $188.00 an ounce on Wednesday morning, its highest-ever official setting. Platinum, at $404.50, matched a recent highest fix nine months ago on August 1, 1996.
As recently as the end of last year, palladium was at a more normal price below $115.
Its all-time traded high was at the end of the 1970s when OPEC oil "shocks'' and fears of inflation lifted gold to record levels and palladium peaked at around $335.00.
But since official London fixings began in 1989, palladium's top price was $181.50, hit when experiments using the metal suggested that "Cold Fusion" might be an inexhaustible source of energy.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, beneficial rains in the Midwest and Plains over the weekend produced a sharp fall in grain and soybean prices as production prospects improved.
Crude oil and wheat prices were somewhat steadier on Wednesday after Tuesday sell-offs. Funds had sold wheat, citing weekend rain in the U.S. plains that would be beneficial to the crops.
The benchmark Brent Blend of North Sea crude oil fell more than 80 cents on Tuesday to around $19.25 per barrel on weakness in U.S. gasoline. It was little changed on Wednesday.
Among the industrial metals, copper was firm, breaching a target on the technical charts at $2,530 per tonne.
